title: RCM Outsourcing Evaluation Playbook: Before You Hand Over the Keys to Your Revenue Cycle
audience: Independent physician practices, from solo to large group, that are evaluating, negotiating, monitoring or leaving an outsourced billing arrangement; described as written for 'independent practice teams'. Practices that already outsource are told to start at Section 5.
summary: Buyer-side guide for independent practices that outsource billing or are thinking about it. It covers the delivery-model choice (in-house, full outsource, hybrid), four vendor types and five fee models, a four-part due-diligence routine, six contract clauses to renegotiate, eight contractual KPI floors, a monthly and quarterly oversight routine, six warning signs, a three-level written escalation ladder, four stress events (new provider, acquisition, payer audit, fast growth) and a 90-day exit plan. Central method: put measurable standards and consequences in the contract, keep direct access to the billing system, recompute the vendor's numbers independently each month, convert every shortfall into dollars, and escalate on a documented timetable. Tools: a 16-criterion selection scorecard, a monthly monitoring form, a 90-day rollout plan and two checklists. No source is cited for any number, and the law governing billing agents is not addressed.

outline.gist: Practices vet a vendor once at signing and then stop measuring, so underperformance hides behind steady deposits; opens with an unsourced market-size figure.

outline.section: Section 1: The Build vs. Buy vs. Outsource Decision
outline.gist: Describes in-house, full-outsource and hybrid models with cost ranges, plus a table matching practice size, denial rate and AR days to a model.
Four vendor types and five fee models with price ranges; tells the reader to compute an all-in effective rate that includes ancillary fees.
Due diligence in four areas: written performance evidence, operations and staffing, reporting transparency, and pointed reference checks; warns about self-serving KPI definitions.
Six clauses to renegotiate: term and auto-renewal, termination fees, data ownership, performance standards, fee-base definition, and the business associate agreement.

outline.section: Section 5: Performance Standards - The KPIs Your Contract Must Require
outline.gist: Defines six KPIs plus two aging limits with contractual floors, then shows three ways to turn a shortfall into dollars.
Seven-item monthly review agenda, insistence on direct system access and independent recalculation, and a quarterly payer- and provider-level deep dive.

outline.section: Section 7: Red Flags - Signs Your Vendor Is Underperforming
outline.gist: Six warning signs: self-defined KPIs, unexplained aging, administrative write-offs, shifting report formats, vendor staff turnover and slow responses.

outline.section: Section 8: The Escalation and Remediation Protocol
outline.gist: Three written levels: notification with root-cause and corrective-plan deadlines, formal remediation with vendor leadership, then performance-based termination.

outline.section: Section 9: Special Situations That Change Your Vendor Relationship
outline.gist: Guidance for adding a provider (credentialing lead times), acquiring a practice, responding to payer audits and outgrowing vendor capacity.

outline.section: Section 10: When to Bring It Back In-House
outline.gist: Five exit triggers and a three-phase 90-day transition: preparation and data extract, parallel operations, then AR hand-off and reconciliation.
Part A scores candidates on 16 criteria from 1 to 5; Part B is a monthly form comparing nine KPIs with contract thresholds.
Month-by-month rollout: assess and recompute KPIs, negotiate and build the monitoring routine, then run the first review and calibrate.
An 18-item pre-signing checklist and a 17-item monthly review checklist covering preparation, the meeting and follow-up.
Restates that results depend on oversight after signing and promotes three other products from the same vendor.
Disclaimers: figures are 'commonly cited' ranges or vendor-observed patterns supposedly labeled as such; no figure in the text is actually labeled or sourced.

framework_elements: All-in vendor cost and effective-rate calculation
Vendor due diligence on written performance evidence
Vendor operations review (credentials, turnover, accounts per biller)
Fee-base definition matched to the NCR definition
Retained direct access to billing system and data
Independent KPI recalculation versus vendor-reported figures
Quarterly deep-dive by payer and provider
Denial reason analysis and aged-denial tracking
Charge lag and claim submission lag monitoring
Three-level escalation with written documentation trail
Revenue-cycle and vendor diligence on an acquired practice
Payer audit response coordination with the vendor
Vendor capacity reassessment during rapid growth
Exit triggers and 90-day billing transition with AR hand-off

processes.name: Delivery-model decision and all-in cost comparison
steps: Total the fully loaded in-house cost: staff pay and benefits, software, clearinghouse, training, management time
Request itemized vendor proposals covering the base rate and every recurring or one-time fee
Divide each vendor's projected monthly cost by actual monthly net collections to get an effective rate
Compare both sides at the practice's real volume and against the size-based table
Choose in-house, full outsource or hybrid and record the reasoning
Revisit the choice in the annual operating review
processes.cadence: At the decision point, then annually

processes.name: Vendor due diligence and scoring
steps: Ask each candidate for written 12-month averages for comparable clients: NCR, first-pass acceptance, days in AR, denial rate by reason, reversal rate
Confirm which KPI definitions the vendor uses
Review staffing: certifications, turnover, accounts per biller, days from charge to claim, denial workflow, platform and security
Establish which reports are standard, how often they arrive, and whether the practice keeps system access
Call same-specialty references, ask for before-and-after numbers and a sample monthly report
Score every candidate on the same 16 criteria and select on verifiable evidence

processes.name: Contract negotiation
steps: Limit the first term to 12 months with annual renewal and a non-renewal notice window of 30 days or less
Add a right to leave without penalty after two straight months below a contracted KPI
State that the practice owns all billing data and that a complete standard-format extract is due within 30 days of notice at no charge
Attach a performance addendum with thresholds, measurement periods and consequences
Define net collections for the fee the same way it is defined for the NCR
Sign a separate business associate agreement
Set a turnaround time for producing audit documentation
processes.cadence: Before signing and at each renewal

processes.name: Monthly vendor performance review
steps: Pull data directly from the practice's own system and recompute the KPIs
Compare with the vendor's reported figures and note every gap
Review AR by aging bucket and flag buckets rising two months running
List the top five denial reasons by count and dollars and confirm the action on each
Demand an explanation for any denial unresolved after 60 days
Check charge lag and submission lag against thresholds
Review all write-offs, separating contractual from administrative
Put a dollar value on any KPI shortfall
Send written notes with commitments and dates; log breaches and issue a Level 1 notice if needed
processes.owner_role: Practice-side owner of the vendor relationship (physician-owner, administrator or in-house billing manager)

processes.name: Quarterly deep-dive
steps: Trend 90 days of KPIs against contract thresholds
Break denials and performance down by payer and by provider
Confirm the vendor applied payer policy and coding updates
If visit volume is growing more than 20% a year, ask whether staffing on the account has scaled
Start the renewal or escalation decision well before the auto-renewal date

processes.name: Three-level escalation and remediation
steps: Level 1, first breach: send written notice stating measured value versus threshold
Require a root-cause analysis within 10 business days and a corrective plan within 20
Level 2, second consecutive month or weak plan: send formal notice to vendor leadership citing the contract
Hold a remediation meeting with leadership; agree weekly checkpoints and a recovery date in writing
Level 3, no recovery: issue termination notice under the performance clause and start the transition
Keep a dated written record of every step
processes.cadence: Event-driven: month one, month two, then sustained breach

processes.name: Vendor exit and 90-day billing transition
steps: Confirm that a documented exit trigger has been met
Days 1-30: give notice, obtain the full data extract, set up the new system or vendor and clearinghouse links, map open AR by bucket and owner
Days 31-60: new operation bills new dates of service while the old vendor works legacy AR; meet weekly with both
Agree when and how open claims transfer
Days 61-90: transfer unresolved claims with history and reconcile counts, payments and balances to the practice's system
Track the first 30 days of KPIs and hold a lessons-learned review
processes.owner_role: Physician-owner or administrator with the incoming billing lead

processes.name: Payer audit response with a billing vendor
steps: Log the letter on receipt: payer, date, scope, deadline
Have the vendor produce claim files and payment history within the contracted turnaround
Compare documentation with each audited claim before anything is sent
Involve the vendor's compliance contact and note how responsive they are
Bring in counsel or a consultant when the audit is large (document's cut-offs: more than 20 claims or $10,000)
Respond by the deadline every time

tools_templates.description: Eighteen pre-signing checks in three groups: performance evidence, contract terms, operational setup.

tools_templates.name: Quick-Reference Checklist 2: Monthly Vendor Performance Review

metrics.name: Net collection rate (NCR)
metrics.definition: Share of collectible revenue (charges after contractual adjustments) that is actually collected; called the master measure of billing performance.
metrics.formula: Total payments ÷ (total charges − contractual write-offs); reported monthly as a rolling 90-day average
metrics.target: 95-98% described as industry standard; contract floor 94% (one worked example treats 96% as the contract standard)
metrics.red_flag: Below 94%: corrective plan due in 30 days; exit without penalty if still below after 60 consecutive days

metrics.name: Clean claim rate (first-pass acceptance)
metrics.definition: Share of claims accepted on first submission with no rejection or denial.
metrics.formula: Implied only: claims accepted first time ÷ claims submitted, monthly

metrics.name: Days in AR
metrics.definition: Average days from date of service to receipt of payment (the document's wording; not the conventional AR-balance-over-daily-charges calculation).
metrics.red_flag: Above 50 days (also used in Section 1 as a signal to outsource)

metrics.name: Denial rate
metrics.definition: Share of submitted claims denied by payers, reported in total and by reason category (medical necessity, eligibility, timely filing, authorization, coding).
metrics.formula: Implied only: denied claims ÷ claims submitted
metrics.red_flag: Above 10% (Section 1 uses a chronic rate above 12% as a signal to outsource)

metrics.name: Denial reversal rate
metrics.definition: Share of denied claims that are appealed or corrected and then paid.
metrics.formula: Implied only: denials overturned and paid ÷ appealable denials, rolling 90 days ('appealable' is not defined)

metrics.name: Claim submission lag
metrics.definition: Average days from date of service (or from charge entry; the document uses both) to first claim submission.
metrics.target: 3 business days from charge entry; contract ceiling 5 business days
metrics.red_flag: Any claim sent more than 14 days after service is to be reported as an outlier

metrics.name: AR over 90 days
metrics.definition: Share of the total AR balance older than 90 days (aging basis not stated).
metrics.formula: Implied only: AR balance over 90 days ÷ total AR balance
metrics.red_flag: Share rising for two or more consecutive months

metrics.name: AR over 120 days
metrics.definition: Share of the total AR balance older than 120 days (aging basis not stated).
metrics.formula: Implied only: AR balance over 120 days ÷ total AR balance
metrics.red_flag: Share rising for two or more consecutive months

metrics.name: Administrative write-off rate
metrics.definition: Write-offs for late filing, missing authorization, missing documentation or medical-necessity failure, as a share of collections.

metrics.name: All-in effective vendor rate
metrics.definition: Everything the vendor charges, expressed as a share of net collections.
metrics.formula: (base fee + clearinghouse, per-claim, per-statement, portal, integration, onboarding and other recurring charges for the month) ÷ monthly net collections
metrics.red_flag: Below 4.5% (scope or service doubt) or above 8% for ordinary primary care

metrics.name: Charge lag
metrics.definition: Days from service to charge entry, reviewed monthly alongside submission lag.

metrics.name: Aged unresolved denials
metrics.definition: Denials open more than 60 days without resolution.
metrics.target: None past 60 days without documented action
metrics.red_flag: Any unexplained denial older than 60 days

metrics.name: Accounts per biller (staff-to-practice ratio)
metrics.definition: Number of client practices each biller or account manager handles.

metrics.name: Account manager turnover
metrics.definition: Changes of account manager or primary biller on the practice's account.
metrics.red_flag: More than one change within 12 months

metrics.name: Visit volume growth
metrics.definition: Annual growth in visits, used as the trigger to re-check vendor capacity.

metrics.name: Vendor-reported versus independently calculated KPI variance
metrics.definition: Difference between the vendor's figures and the practice's own calculation from its system.

metrics.name: NCR gap in dollars
metrics.definition: Annual revenue attributed to an NCR shortfall.
metrics.formula: Annual adjusted charges × (contract NCR − actual NCR)

metrics.name: Excess denial cost
metrics.definition: Annual revenue attributed to denials above the contract ceiling that are never recovered.
metrics.formula: (actual denial rate − ceiling) × monthly claims × (1 − reversal rate) × average claim value × 12

metrics.name: Probability-weighted AR value
metrics.definition: AR balance discounted by an assumed collectability factor per aging bucket, compared with its value at the current-bucket factor.
metrics.formula: Sum of bucket balance × factor (90% current, 70% 30-60 days, 55% 61-90, 40% 91-120, 20% over 120)

metrics.name: Vendor selection score
metrics.definition: Sum of 1-5 ratings across 16 selection criteria.
metrics.formula: Sum of ratings (maximum 80); heavier weighting of evidence and infrastructure is suggested but no weights are given

metrics.name: Top five denial reasons
metrics.definition: Monthly ranking of denial reason codes by count and by dollar amount.

metrics.name: Vendor response time
metrics.definition: How long the vendor takes to answer practice questions and close review items.
metrics.red_flag: Answers that take days, missing follow-up, incomplete replies

numeric_claims.claim: The RCM outsourcing market generated approximately $32 billion in 2024 and is projected to exceed $100 billion by the early 2030s
In-house billing staff cost $45,000-$70,000 per biller annually in salary and benefits
Full in-house billing makes most sense typically above $3-$4 million in annual collections
Full-outsource fee typically 4-9% of net collections; current market average 5.5-7.2% for full-service billing
Full outsource is most appropriate for solo and small group practices, typically under $2 million in annual collections
Size table: solo under $1M full outsource; 2-4 providers $1-3M outsource or hybrid; 5-10 providers $3-7M hybrid or in-house; 10+ providers over $7M in-house
A chronic denial rate above 12% or AR above 50 days signals outsourcing or a hybrid with a cleanup mandate
Full-service national RCM companies are typically priced at 5-8% of net collections
Specialty-specific billing companies charge 6-9% for complex specialties
Small local or regional billing services often fall in the 4-7% range
Clearinghouse, statement, claim, software and onboarding fees can add 1-2 points above the stated rate
Per-claim flat rates typically run $3-$10 per claim
Hourly billing work ranges $25-$65 per hour
Full-service RCM should cost 5.5-7.5% of net collections all-in in 2025-2026; below 4.5% warrants scrutiny; above 8% is above market for standard primary care
More than 20 client practices per biller is a red flag
Most standard RCM contracts run one to three years with auto-renewal; non-renewal notice is typically due 60-90 days before renewal
Early termination fees are often three to six months of average vendor fees; a practice 18 months into a three-year contract may face $30,000-$60,000
Net collection rate industry standard for a well-managed independent practice is 95-98%; contract minimum 94%
Clean claim rate industry standard is 95-98% first-pass acceptance; below 90% indicates systematic preparation errors
Days in AR industry standard is 30-40 days; above 50 days indicates systematic delays
Denial rate below 5% is strong, 5-10% acceptable, above 10% indicates systemic problems
Minimum 65% reversal on appealable denials; a reversal rate below 50% means collectible revenue is being written off
Industry standard is claim submission within 3 business days of charge entry; contract maximum 5 business days
AR over 90 days should be no more than 15% of total AR; AR over 120 days no more than 10%
AR past 120 days collects below 40% for commercial payers and below 20% for some government payers; bucket factors roughly 90%, 70%, 55%, 40%, 20%
Administrative write-offs above 1-2% of collections warrant detailed investigation
An unmeasured 3-5% NCR gap on $2 million of annual collections is $60,000-$100,000 a year, $180,000-$300,000 over a three-year contract
Credentialing takes 60-90 days for Medicare, 60-120 for Medicaid, 30-90 for commercial payers and 90-180 for hospital-based credentialing; start at least 90 days before the first patient
Engage an attorney or consultant if an audit involves more than 20 claims or potential recoupment above $10,000
A billing transition needs at least 90 days; a well-run new operation reaches full performance within 60-90 days; growth above 20% a year in visits calls for a capacity reassessment

checkable_claims.claim: During the credentialing period, claims can often be submitted under a supervising provider's NPI, but this requires explicit verification with each payer [and documented supervision].
checkable_claims.why: For Medicare this is allowed only under narrow incident-to or substitute-physician rules and never for hospital or skilled nursing facility visits. A facility-based practice that follows it when adding a clinician would be filing false claims and owe repayment.

checkable_claims.claim: Until a provider is fully credentialed with every relevant payer, their claims cannot be submitted under their NPI.
checkable_claims.why: Medicare ties the billing effective date to the application filing date and allows limited retrospective billing, so early visits are held, not lost. Believing otherwise forfeits revenue or pushes the practice toward the risky NPI workaround.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicare: 60–90 days from complete application submission ... The credentialing process must begin at least 90 days before a new provider sees their first patient.
checkable_claims.why: Hiring and start dates depend on real contractor processing times and on how early an enrollment application may be filed; a wrong lead time delays cash or gets the application returned.

checkable_claims.claim: Never ignore an audit letter. Non-response is treated as an admission and triggers automatic recoupment.
checkable_claims.section: Section 9: A Payer or RAC Audit
checkable_claims.why: The real consequence of a missed records deadline (denial for no documentation, overpayment demand, appeal rights, limits on recoupment during appeal) shapes the response; calling it an admission misstates the practice's rights.

checkable_claims.claim: An RCM vendor without a current BAA is not HIPAA-compliant, and using them exposes the practice to HIPAA liability. It should be a standalone agreement, not embedded in the service contract.
checkable_claims.section: Section 4: HIPAA and Business Associate Agreement
checkable_claims.why: The practice runs billing through AI agents under a business associate agreement and would itself become a business associate if it sold services; it needs the actual HIPAA contract requirements, not a drafting preference stated as a rule.

checkable_claims.claim: The vendor's fee typically ranges from 4–9% of net collections ... with the current market average tracking between 5.5% and 7.2% for full-service billing across practice types.
checkable_claims.why: This is the outside-market comparator for the practice's own cost to collect and the price anchor for any service the owner might sell; an invented range would distort both decisions.

checkable_claims.claim: AR that ages past 120 days has collection probability below 40% for commercial payers and below 20% for some government payers.
checkable_claims.section: Section 5: Calculating the Cost of a KPI Gap (AR Aging Cost)
checkable_claims.why: Collectability factors drive AR valuation in monthly reporting and in a sale. Medicare claims stay payable inside the one-year filing limit, so unsupported decay factors could misprice receivables or excuse early write-offs.

checkable_claims.claim: Medicaid: 60–120 days, with significant state variation; Commercial payers: 30–90 days, depending on payer and network status; Hospital-based credentialing: 90–180 days.
checkable_claims.why: Medicare Advantage, Florida Medicaid plan and hospital privileging lead times decide when a new clinician produces collectible revenue; a 30-day commercial assumption would understate the cash gap when the practice hires.

adopt.idea: Recompute billing KPIs every month from raw practice-management data under written definitions, by someone other than whoever does the billing, and reconcile the result to the operator's own report.
adopt.why: Self-reported performance is the weak point of any delegated billing function, whether the operator is a vendor, an employee or software.
adopt.note: Run an independent check on the AI agents' output straight from AdvancedMD reports; the agents should not grade their own work.

adopt.idea: Write a one-page billing performance standard: each KPI with an exact formula, data source, measurement window, floor and the action a breach triggers.
adopt.why: Thresholds only bind when the definition is fixed; undefined metrics can be made to look good.
adopt.note: Replace the document's loose definitions and recalibrate for a Medicare fee-for-service, facility-based mix; the days-in-AR and lag ceilings probably should be tighter than 45 days and 5 business days.

adopt.idea: Hold a fixed-agenda monthly billing review (KPIs, aging, top denial reasons, aged denials, lag, write-offs, open items) and a quarterly deep dive by payer and provider.
adopt.why: A standing agenda turns billing oversight into an operating rhythm and builds a KPI history.
adopt.note: Fits the owner-as-CFO role; cut payer views by Medicare, each Medicare Advantage plan, Medicaid plans, VA and Tricare, and by physician versus nurse practitioner.

adopt.idea: Review all write-offs monthly, splitting contractual adjustments from avoidable ones (late filing, missing authorization or documentation) and requiring a reason and sign-off for the avoidable kind.
adopt.why: Avoidable write-offs are where lost revenue hides, and miscoded adjustments can inflate the net collection rate.
adopt.note: Set an owner-approval rule for avoidable write-offs proposed by AI agents and track timely-filing losses in dollars.

adopt.idea: Translate every KPI shortfall into monthly and annual dollars before acting on it.
adopt.why: Dollar figures set priorities and make the business case; percentages do not.
adopt.note: At roughly $1.0-1.1 million of net revenue each NCR point is about $10,000-11,000 a year. Use allowed amounts rather than billed charges and treat the result as an estimate. Calibrate any aging discount factors from the practice's own payment history by payer, not the document's.

adopt.idea: Keep ownership of the billing system licence, the data, and the clearinghouse and payer-portal credentials, and require a documented export and exit path from every vendor.
adopt.why: Whoever controls system access and data controls the practice's cash flow and its ability to switch.
adopt.note: Already true for the practice's AdvancedMD instance; apply the same test to the AI vendor, the clearinghouse and any future billing partner.

adopt.idea: Compute the practice's own all-in cost to collect and compare it with what an outsourced vendor would charge at the same volume.
adopt.why: It tests whether the in-house model is earning its keep and gives a normalized billing cost for a valuation.
adopt.note: If the document's unverified 5.5-7.5% range holds, the outside comparator is roughly $55,000-83,000 a year at this revenue. Count AI subscriptions, software, clearinghouse and owner time on the in-house side.

adopt.idea: Use a time-boxed escalation ladder: written notice, root cause in 10 business days, corrective plan in 20, leadership-level remediation in month two, exit if not fixed, with everything documented.
adopt.why: Deadlines and a paper trail stop performance problems from drifting and support enforcement.
adopt.note: There is no billing vendor to escalate to, but the same ladder works for AI-agent error incidents and for the software, clearinghouse and credentialing vendors.

adopt.idea: Before buying a practice, pull 12 months of its AR aging, check for open audits or payer investigations, benchmark its collection and denial rates, verify clinician enrollment status, and decide deliberately what happens to its billing arrangement.
adopt.why: Billing defects and vendor contracts transfer with the deal and affect price and working capital.
adopt.note: Relevant to a growth-by-acquisition path and, in mirror image, to what a buyer will ask of this practice.

adopt.idea: Treat this playbook as the buyer's requirements list when designing a billing or optimization service: 12-month terms, measurable service levels, client-owned data with a 30-day export, performance-based exit and all-in pricing.
adopt.why: Informed clients will ask for these terms; offering them up front differentiates a new entrant.
adopt.note: Only relevant if the owner launches a service for other practices. Counsel must add the billing-agent, percentage-fee and business-associate rules the document leaves out.

practice_relevance.why: The practice does not outsource billing; AI agents run it in-house on the practice's own AdvancedMD system under a business associate agreement. Vendor selection, termination-fee negotiation and the bring-it-back-in-house plan therefore have no immediate use. What transfers is the control method: written KPI definitions and floors, monthly independent recalculation, write-off review, dollar-valued gaps and a documented escalation path apply directly to governing AI billing agents. The pricing section supplies the outside-market comparator for cost to collect (unverified). The acquisition checklist and credentialing lead times matter for growth, and the whole document reads as the buyer's requirements list if the owner builds a service for other practices. Nothing is tailored to Medicare fee-for-service, facility-based work, crossover claims or a practice with almost no patient collections; Medicare is mentioned once.
sections_that_do_not_apply: Section 1 size-based table: no row for software- or AI-run in-house billing, which is how the practice operates
Section 2 vendor types and fee models: no procurement under way; useful only as a price benchmark
Section 3 vendor selection and reference checks
Section 4 auto-renewal and early-termination-fee negotiation (transferable only by analogy to software and AI vendor contracts)
Section 8 Levels 2 and 3 (vendor leadership remediation and termination)
Section 10 transition from a vendor back in-house
Section 9 supervising-NPI workaround: not usable for Medicare hospital and skilled nursing facility visits
Section 5 thresholds as written: 45-day AR and 8% denial ceilings are not calibrated to a Medicare-heavy, facility-based payer mix
Per-statement and patient-portal fee items: the practice has almost no patient-pay volume

accuracy_concerns: Section 9 presents billing a not-yet-credentialed clinician under a 'supervising' provider's NPI as a workaround that 'can often' be used. For Medicare that is lawful only inside narrow incident-to rules (non-institutional setting, direct supervision, physician-established plan of care) or substitute-physician arrangements; incident-to does not exist for hospital or skilled nursing facility visits, and many Medicare Advantage and commercial plans forbid the practice outright. Treating it as routine is a false-claims risk that the hedge about checking with each payer does not cure.

The same section says claims cannot go out until the clinician is credentialed with every payer and stops there. It omits that Medicare sets the billing effective date at the later of the application filing date or first service date and permits up to 30 days of retrospective billing (42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a)), so services are held and billed after approval rather than lost. Payer-by-payer retroactivity is not discussed.

Medicare enrollment in '60-90 days' is a folk number, not a rule, and nothing is cited. The instruction to start at least 90 days ahead does not account for the contractor practice (in CMS transmittals and on First Coast's enrollment pages) of returning individual-practitioner applications filed more than 60 days before the requested effective date; preparation can start early, the Medicare filing cannot.

'Non-response is treated as an admission and triggers automatic recoupment' is wrong in form. Ignoring a records request leads to denial of the sampled claims for lack of documentation and an overpayment demand; the practice keeps its appeal rights and Medicare recoupment is limited while timely first- and second-level appeals are pending. The advice to always respond is right; the stated reason is not.

Days in AR is defined as the average time from service to payment, with no formula. The conventional measure is AR balance divided by average daily charges. A document that warns about vendors using non-standard definitions writes one into its own model contract.

Clean claim rate is defined as acceptance with no rejection or denial, which is first-pass payment rather than the usual front-end acceptance measure, and that makes the 95% floor arithmetically incompatible with the 8% denial ceiling in the same table.

NCR is to be measured on a rolling 90-day window with no instruction to match payments to the charges that produced them, so the figure will swing with volume changes and cannot support a 60-day termination clock.

Every threshold is blind to payer mix and specialty. For a mostly Medicare fee-for-service practice (clean electronic claims payable from day 14) a 45-day AR ceiling and a 5-business-day submission allowance are lax; elsewhere they may be tight. No adjustment method is offered.

The aging-bucket collectability factors (90/70/55/40/20%) and the statement about balances over 120 days have no source and look invented. Medicare claims do not lose value on that curve inside the one-year filing limit.

All price points (4-9%, 5.5-7.2%, 5.5-7.5% all-in, $3-10 per claim, $25-65 per hour, $45,000-70,000 per biller) are unsourced. The 5.5-7.2% figure could not be traced in a quick search; public commentary, mostly vendor marketing, clusters around 4-10% with 5-8% typical.

The $32 billion market figure matches one market-research publisher's global 2024 estimate (IMARC, about $109 billion forecast for 2033); the document does not name it and other publishers give different bases.
'Flat monthly fee ... common in government/Medicaid contracting' is an unexplained assertion with no evident basis for physician-practice billing.
A standalone business associate agreement is presented as the correct form. HIPAA requires the business-associate terms but not a separate document; this is a drafting preference stated like a rule.

The NCR-gap figure is called arithmetic rather than an estimate. It is an estimate: it assumes the whole gap is recoverable and attributable to the vendor. The denial example uses an undefined 'average claim value' (billed or allowed?) and a 50% reversal rate that is below the document's own 65% floor.

Vendor risk is framed only as under-collection. A percentage-of-collections fee also rewards over-billing, and the practice, not the vendor, answers for claims filed under its name. The proposed contract has no coding-accuracy standard, audit right or compliance duty.

The cut-offs for calling a lawyer in an audit (more than 20 claims or $10,000) are arbitrary, ignore extrapolation from small samples, and treat a consultant as interchangeable with counsel, which gives up privilege.
'Most standard RCM contracts contain no enforceable performance standards' and 'above 20 practices per biller is a red flag' are generalizations with no data behind them.

Reviewer note on the basis for these concerns: regulation pages could not be opened directly in this session (www.ecfr.gov and www.law.cornell.edu are outside the allowed network), so the citations above rest on search-result excerpts and prior knowledge and should be confirmed in the verification track.
internal_contradictions: NCR contract floor is 94% in the KPI list, the summary table and the scorecard, but the worked example in the same section calls 96% 'the contractual standard'.
Clean claim rate must be at least 95% with no rejection or denial, while the same table tolerates a denial rate of up to 8%; both cannot be met.

Text, checklist and 90-day plan speak of 'six KPIs'; the Section 5 table has eight rows and the Part B form has nine, including an administrative write-off 'contracted threshold' that Section 5 never defines.
Administrative write-off trigger is stated three ways: above 1-2% (Section 7), 2% or less (Part B), over 1% (Checklist 2).
The closing disclaimer says figures are labeled as industry benchmark or 'CCRx-observed' throughout; no figure in the text carries either label and the term appears only in the disclaimer.
The denial-cost example says the Red Flags section applies 'the same arithmetic'; that section actually uses an NCR-gap calculation.
Section 1 is titled 'Build vs. Buy vs. Outsource' but describes in-house, full outsource and hybrid; no 'buy' option exists.

Full outsourcing is said to suit practices under $2 million, yet the table splits at $1 million and $3 million; a rate below 4.5% 'warrants scrutiny' although the document's own range for small local vendors starts at 4%.
Headline market average is given as 5.5-7.2% and hidden fees are said to add 1-2 points, yet the all-in market reference is only 5.5-7.5%.
Early termination fees are described in one sentence as a multiple of average monthly collections and as months of average vendor fees, which differ by more than tenfold.
The 90-day plan refers to a 'Section 4 checklist'; Section 4 has none.

Exit timing differs by section: two consecutive months of breach (Section 4), 60 days below threshold after a 30-day plan (Section 5), or only after a Level 2 remediation plan begun in month two has run (Section 8).
Balances past 120 days are said to collect below 40% for commercial payers, but the factor list gives 40% for 91-120 days and 20% beyond 120.
A non-renewal window of 30 days or less is recommended alongside a transition said to need at least 90 days, with no transition-services clause to bridge the gap.
time_sensitive_or_outdated: Fee ranges are labeled as 2025-2026 market conditions and will drift; none has a source to refresh against.
The market-size figure is a 2024 estimate with a forecast; marketing colour, not a planning input.
Credentialing lead times are undated generalities; Medicare contractor processing and plan timelines change and differ by payer and state.

The audit discussion centres on Recovery Audit Contractors. For a Part B physician practice in 2026 the likelier contacts are the Medicare contractor's targeted probe-and-educate reviews, program-integrity contractors and Medicare Advantage plan record requests, none of which is named.
A product generated in September 2026 offers only staff-run in-house billing, full outsourcing or a hybrid; software- or AI-agent-run billing is absent.
Nothing reflects the 2024 national clearinghouse outage (vendor and clearinghouse continuity, backup submission routes) or current expectations for verifying a business associate's security.
Silent on the overpayment report-and-return duty, whose standard was revised effective 2025.
The biller cost range carries no year or locality.
ai_generation_signals: No author, credential, client or data source anywhere; 'operational experience across independent practices' is asserted only in a disclaimer.
Disclaimer promises labels ('CCRx-observed') that the text never uses.
Formulaic contrast sentences repeated throughout ('not a threat, it is...', 'not bureaucracy, it is...', 'not a luxury, it is...') and roughly 207 em dashes in 38 pages.
Broken internal references: a 'Section 4 checklist' that does not exist, a cross-reference to arithmetic Section 7 does not contain, and a 'buy' option in a title with no content.
Counts that do not match their own lists (six KPIs versus eight and nine rows).
Oddly precise unsourced ranges (5.5-7.2%) beside round rules of thumb (20 practices per biller, 20 claims, $10,000, 20% growth).
Identical callout-box pattern in every section; tagline and web address repeated four times.
Seven cross-references to four other products in the same catalogue stand in for missing detail (KPI formulas, staffing costs, technology selection).
Marketing hook ('the framework the vendor does not want you to have') wrapped around standard procurement advice.
Medicare appears once in the entire text, in a credentialing bullet; no regulation, form or agency is named.
missing_for_real_use: Exact KPI formulas and data rules: days in AR, service-date-matched NCR, denial rate basis (claims or lines, count or dollars, rejections in or out), aging basis, and what counts as 'appealable'.

The documents it tells the reader to create: performance addendum wording, model contract clauses, Level 1-3 notice letters, a KPI tracking workbook and an in-house versus vendor cost worksheet. The scorecard has no weights or pass mark.

Billing-agent law: Medicare's payment-to-agent conditions (42 CFR 424.73 and 424.80) and the Medicaid counterpart (42 CFR 447.10), which restrict paying program money to an agent whose fee is a percentage of billings or collections, so deposits must land in an account the practice controls; bank, lockbox and deposit controls; state fee-splitting and billing-company rules. Confirm details with counsel.

Any statement that the practice remains liable for what the vendor submits, together with coding-accuracy standards, audit rights, who may change codes or modifiers, exclusion-list screening of vendor staff, and the federal compliance guidance for third-party billing companies.
Overpayment handling: credit balances, refund timeliness and the 60-day report-and-return duty when a vendor error is found.

Security and continuity terms: breach-notice timing, subcontractor flow-down, security attestations, cyber and errors-and-omissions insurance, indemnity and liability caps, clearinghouse-outage contingency and return of data. It also misses that federal HIPAA guidance (OCR FAQ 2074) treats a business associate blocking a practice's access to its data over a fee dispute as an impermissible use.

Offshore work and data location, including Florida's 2023 rule (s. 408.051) that patient information held by providers using certified record systems be stored in the United States, its territories or Canada, and Medicare Advantage plans' offshore-subcontractor disclosure requirements.

Shared-accountability carve-outs every vendor will demand (denials caused by the practice's documentation, eligibility or enrollment lapses), a baseline period, and payer-mix adjustment of thresholds.

Exit mechanics: the fee owed on legacy AR collected after termination, lead times to re-enroll electronic claims, remittances and funds transfer under a new submitter, and ownership of clearinghouse and portal credentials.

KPIs it never mentions: payment-posting lag and accuracy, unapplied cash, credit-balance aging, rejection turnaround, underpayment detection against fee schedules, secondary and crossover billing, timely-filing write-offs in dollars, charge-capture completeness.
Actual filing and appeal deadlines by payer, and Medicare audit types, response windows, appeal levels and recoupment limits.
Any treatment of software- or AI-run billing, or of how to oversee automated billing agents.
